name: The Categorical Imperative
plain_explanation: Kant's rule for right action: act only in the way you could will everyone else to act, as if your personal rule of action were a universal law of nature -- not because of what results it produces, but simply because it is the rational, dutiful thing to do.
precise_definition: A synthetic a priori command of reason, unconditional and independent of any particular end (unlike the 'hypothetical imperative', which is conditional on a desired goal): 'Act only according to a maxim by which you can at the same time will that it shall become a general law.' Moral worth requires acting from a sense of duty, not merely in accordance with duty.
why_it_mattered: It grounds Kant's rejection of utilitarianism and of any ethics that derives morality from an external purpose, making duty (not consequences or inclination) the sole basis of moral worth; it also underlies Kant's principle that every man should be treated as an end in himself.
examples: Borrowing money is wrong because if everyone did so there would be no money left to lend
Theft and murder similarly fail the test of universalizability
objections: It gives, at best, a necessary but not sufficient criterion of virtue: some acts Kant would clearly judge wrong (e.g. suicide) cannot obviously be shown wrong by the maxim, since a melancholic could consistently will universal suicide.

Treating every man as an absolute end in himself makes it impossible, if taken literally, to resolve conflicts of interest between people -- a problem especially acute in political philosophy, which requires some principle for deciding whose interests yield.
It can be salvaged by reinterpreting the 'end in himself' principle as meaning all men should count equally in decisions affecting many, which gives it an ethical basis compatible with democracy.
competing_positions: Utilitarianism, which Kant explicitly rejects, judging actions by consequences rather than by the universalizability of their governing maxim
influence_on_later_thinkers: Remains, per Russell, familiar 'outside the circle of professional philosophers' as a phrase, and has considerable historical importance in ethics.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Can be read as an abstract form of the doctrine of the rights of man, and, reinterpreted, as an ethical basis for democracy.
